members.statement_original:
Let $\mathcal B$ be the collection of linear operators $\{f\otimes g:f\in\mathcal H_U,g\in\mathcal H_\Theta\}$. Thus, each member of $\mathcal B$ is a linear operator mapping from $\mathcal H_\Theta$ to $\mathcal H_U$ such that, for any $h\in\mathcal H_\Theta$, $(f\otimes g)(h)=f\langle g,h\rangle_{\mathcal H_\Theta}$. Let $\mathcal S$ be the linear span of $\mathcal B$, consisting of finite linear combinations of members of $\mathcal B$ with real coefficients. Define in $\mathcal S$ the inner product
\[
\langle\alpha_1(f_1\otimes g_1)+\cdots+\alpha_r(f_r\otimes g_r),\widetilde\alpha_1(\widetilde f_1\otimes\widetilde g_1)+\cdots+\widetilde\alpha_r(\widetilde f_s\otimes\widetilde g_s)\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^r\sum_{j=1}^s\alpha_i\widetilde\alpha_j\langle f_i,\widetilde f_j\rangle_{\mathcal H_U}\langle g_i,\widetilde g_j\rangle_{\mathcal H_\Theta}.
\]
Endowed with this inner product, $\mathcal S$ is an inner product space; its completion as a Hilbert space is the tensor product space $\mathcal H_U\otimes\mathcal H_\Theta$.

members.statement_original: Recall that a kernel $\kappa$ is characteristic if the mapping $P\mapsto\int\kappa(\cdot,X)\,dP$ is injective. Here, the dot notation $\int\kappa(\cdot,X)\,dP$ simply means the function $x\mapsto\int\kappa(x,X)\,dP$. So $\kappa$ being characteristic means if $\int\kappa(x,X)\,dP_1=\int\kappa(x,X)\,dP_2$ for all $x$ then $P_1=P_2$.

\[
\operatorname{Arctan}(x,y)=\begin{cases}
\arctan(y/x),&x>0,\\
\arctan(y/x)+\pi,&x<0,y\ge0,\\
\arctan(y/x)-\pi,&x<0,y<0,\\
\pi/2,&x=0,y>0,\\
-\pi/2,&x=0,y<0.
\end{cases}
\]

In the following, we use $S_j$ to denote the Euclidean norm of the vector $(v_j,\ldots,v_d)^\top$.
The following function from $\Omega_\Theta$ to $S^{d-1}$
\[
v_1=\sin\theta_1,\quad v_2=\cos\theta_1\sin\theta_2,\quad\ldots,\quad v_{d-1}=\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2\cdots\cos\theta_{d-2}\sin\theta_{d-1},\quad v_d=\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2\cdots\cos\theta_{d-2}\cos\theta_{d-1}.
\]
(2.6)
is bijective with inverse
\[
\theta_j=\begin{cases}\operatorname{Arctan}(S_{j+1},v_j),&j=1,\ldots,d-2,\\\operatorname{Arctan}(v_d,v_{d-1}),&j=d-1.\end{cases}
\]
(2.7)
We will denote the first function (2.6) as $v=\rho(\theta)$ and the second function (2.7) as $\theta=g(v)$. Then $x=uv=u\rho(\theta)\equiv\tau(u,\theta)$.

members.statement_original:
Let $\mathcal F$ denote the class of all distributions on $(\Omega_X,\mathcal F_X)$. Let $\mathcal H$ be a generic Hilbert space. Let $T:\mathcal F\to\mathcal H$ be a mapping — such mappings are known as statistical functionals. Endow $\mathcal F$ with the uniform metric, and $\mathcal H$ with the metric induced by its inner product. Let $F_0$ be a member of $\mathcal F$. Then $T$ is Frechet differentiable at $F_0$ if there is a linear operator $A:\mathcal F\to\mathcal H$ such that
\[
\lim_{\|F-F_0\|_{\mathcal F}\to0}\frac{\|T(F)-T(F_0)-A(F-F_0)\|_{\mathcal H}}{\|F-F_0\|_{\mathcal F}}=0.
\]

Suppose that $F\mapsto U(x,F)$, $F\mapsto V(x,F)$ and $F\mapsto\Theta(x,F)$ are Frechet differentiable at $F_0$. Let
\[
A_1(x)=-\frac{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}}{[(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)]^{1/2}},\qquad A_2(x)=-\frac{[(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}]\otimes[(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}]}{2[(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)]^{1/2}},
\]
\[
B_1(x)=-\frac{\Sigma^{-1/2}(x-\mu)A_1(x)}{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}-\frac{\Sigma^{-1/2}}{[(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)]^{1/2}},
\]
\[
B_2(x)=-\frac{\Sigma^{-1/2}(x-\mu)A_2(x)}{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}-\frac{[(x-\mu)^\top\otimes I_d](\Sigma^{1/2}\otimes\Sigma+\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^{1/2})^{-1}}{[(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)]^{1/2}},
\]
\[
C_i(x)=[\partial g(V(x))/\partial v^\top]B_i(x),\quad i=1,2,
\]
(5.6)
where $\partial g(V(x))/\partial v^\top$ is the matrix given by Lemma 3. Then, the influence functions of $U(x,F)$, $V(x,F)$ and $\Theta(x,F)$ are
\[
U^\star(x,z)=A_1(x)\mu^\star(z)+A_2(x)\operatorname{vec}[\Sigma^\star(z)],
\]
(5.7)
\[
V^\star(x,z)=B_1(x)\mu^\star(z)+B_2(x)\operatorname{vec}[\Sigma^\star(z)],
\]
(5.8)
\[
\Theta^\star(x,z)=C_1(x)\mu^\star(z)+C_2(x)\operatorname{vec}[\Sigma^\star(z)].
\]
(5.9)

members.statement_original:
Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be an i.i.d. sample of $X$. For a function $A(x)$, we use $E_nA(X)$ to denote the sample average of $A(X_1),\ldots,A(X_n)$. Let $\widehat\mu$ and $\widehat\Sigma$ denote the sample mean and sample variance; that is, $\widehat\mu=E_n(X)$ and $\widehat\Sigma=E_n[(X-\widehat\mu)(X-\widehat\mu)^\top]$.
\[
\widehat W(x)=\widehat\Sigma^{-1/2}(x-\widehat\mu),\quad\widehat U(x)=\|\widehat W(x)\|,\quad\widehat V(x)=\widehat W(x)/\widehat U(x),\quad\widehat\Theta(x)=g(\widehat V(x)).
\]
